Corrective Maintenance. a. Maintenance Management Automated Information System (MMAIS) Management.

As Navy MMAIS applications (MDS, AWN, Electronic Tag Out (eTagOut) and Electronic Shift Operations Management Solution programs) evolve into a connected group of systems, criteria for the management of unit, shipboard and ashore databases and a process for submitting account requests for these MMAIS systems is hereby established. b. Operating Policy for Unit or Shipboard Databases afloat. (1) Will be managed locally by an assigned and designated administrator. (2) Account structures and role or privileges will utilize the TYCOM approved Privilege Matrix which is maintained by the TYCOM. (3) Systems settings will be set to local time not Zulu time for all processing. (4) No outside activity will be allowed direct access to the databases. Database copies require prior written TYCOM N43 approval. (5) All work candidate, job, JSN, pre-2K to 2K review and approvals along with sending of parts requests to supply will be conducted by the ships force, no outside activities will approve work candidate, job, JSN, pre-2K to 2K or shipboard parts. No outside activity will write work candidates directly into a ships force MDS system. All outside activity reporting or finding discrepancies will produce the required “bulkload” per this manual. c. Operating Policy for Unit or Shipboard Databases ashore. (1) All user access levels and accounts will be tracked by the activity creating the account. (2) Every TYCOM will have at a minimum a primary and secondary account manager. Account manager names will be provided to the Navy Enterprise Service Desk (NESD). (3) Users with accounts missing the required forms will be deactivated until the required documentation is presented to the NESD, and the account is approved by the TYCOM. d. Organizational Maintenance Management System - Next Generation (OMMS-NG). Organizational Maintenance Management System - Next Generation is the shipboard program used to document and track material deficiencies in the command. Only active jobs are maintained in the database and are tracked to completion. 3MC will upline a minimum of twice a week to VSB via the RADWEB service.

While the OMMS database contains all active jobs for the ship, “L” and “Z” jobs will not display in the ships database. “L” jobs are work candidates the Port Engineer wrote for work to be completed on the ship. “Z” jobs are ICMP task to be accomplished by outside activities. (1) Up-line Reporting. Up-line reporting via Revised Alternative Data Flow Website (RADWEB) is required at a minimum of twice per calendar week. Platforms on any other MDS, units will verify twice a week that automatic data transfer is occurring. (2) Automated Shore Interface Processing. Automated Shore Interface (ASI) download and processing is required when the ASI record count in RADWEB is 3,000 records for Guided Missile Cruiser (CG), Guided-Missile Destroyer (DDG), Mine Countermeasure Ship, Littoral Combat Ship (LCS), Amphibious Transport Dock, Dock Landing Ship, Patrol Craft (PC), or shore facilities. For Amphibious Assault Ships, Landing Helicopter Dock and Amphibious Command Ships class ASI download and processing is required when the ASI record count in RADWEB is 10,000 records. ASI download and processing for all MDS, of all available ASI records in RADWEB is required when the unit is getting underway for a period of two weeks or longer, monthly at a minimum, and as directed by the TYCOM. Ship’s ASIs available in RADWEB will be downloaded and processed into the ship’s MDS within seven days of ASI creation. (3) Bulkloads and Database Transfer. A bulkload is a CSMP load (work candidate(s) provided as an external file to be loaded into the ship’s CSMP) by the 3MC produced by any outside activity (any person not ships force, no activity will leave a list of material discrepancies or tell the ship to write the work candidate/jobs.). Bulkload files are sent to the 3MC by TYCOM N43. COMNAVSURFPAC or COMNAVSURFLANT N43 3-M is the only authorizing activity for bulkload reviews.

Commands will not transfer, copy, or allow the direct access to or copying of the MDS and or supply database by any outside activity. COMNAVSURFPAC or COMNAVSURFLANT N43 3- M will direct via written permission for database copies. Upon completion of bulkload, the command must review all work candidates to ensure the recommended solution and type availability are accurate. If not accurate, the command should assign to the appropriate TA Code (1-Depot, 2-IMA, 3-Tech Assist) and update the recommended solution. f. Automated Work Notification - AWN is the shipboard program used to document and track material deficiencies in the command. All active jobs and jobs closed within the last year are maintained in the database and are tracked to completion. Upline in AWN are not required as the program uplines automatically. (1) Verifying AWN health. To ensure automatic replication from ship to shore in AWN, utilize TYCOM provided AWN health process guide. AWN health should be verified daily, a minimum of twice weekly, in the shore AWN (ATM) program. (2) AWN Parts Approval for LCS Units. Although parts request, queue, and approval are conducted on the ship, parts will not be ordered until the Work Candidate is approved (changed from pre 2-Kilo to 2-Kilo) in the Shore ATM Database. Once the Work Candidate is made a 2-Kilo, material requisitions can be released to R-Supply Ashore. (3) Automated Shore Interface Processing. Ship’s ASIs available in RADWEB will be downloaded and processed into the ship’s AWN and R-Supply within seven days of ASI creation. For LCS unit, ASI will be processed into the ship’s AWN, shore AWN (ATM), and R-Supply within 7 days of ASI creation. (4) AWN Bulkload process. TYCOM N43 will load Bulkload files directly to Ashore AWN (ATM). The uploaded jobs wills replicate to the AWN database upon completion.

Ship’s 3MC is to monitor the AWN database to ensure the bulkloaded files are received on the ship. f. Validation Screening and Brokering. The master CSMP database for all US Navy ships. The program utilized by Port Engineers to screen and broker or refer work as required. VSB is updated by OMMS and provides status updates to the Open Architecture and Retrieval System (OARS). All jobs TA 1 - 4 are reported to VSB although only TA 1 - 3 will be screened by the Port Engineer. The status of all jobs in VSB are annotated by the “WN Status” field. g. Open Architecture and Retrieval System (OARS). The 3-M history file for all US Navy ships and shore commands. All jobs written by the ship or outside activity will be maintained within the OARS database from the time the command is commissioned until decommissioning. A weekly report from OARS is generated and disbursed to ship via a SPEAR file. The SPEAR file will contain a list of all active jobs and ICMP task assigned to the unit. Life Cycle Of A Work Candidate. A Work candidate is created either on the ship by ship’s force or by an outside maintenance activity. When a job is created by a maintenance activity or inspection team, they create a list of jobs and send them to TYCOM for review. After TYCOM review, the job will be sent to the ship via bulkload to update the ship’s CSMP. A ship uploads the jobs to VSB via upline where the Port Engineer will screen and broker work to the maintenance activities during availabilities as shown in Figure 19-6-1 of this chapter. Key Component Of A Work Candidate. a. Maintenance and Modernization Business Unit (MMBU) Code. A MMBU code (also known as Job Originator Values) is used to identify the outside activity that originated the job. It is identified by the first character in the job sequence number. For example, Job CA01-L001 has a MMBU code of “L” which identifies the Port Engineer as the originator of the job.

CA01-R001 has a MMBU code of “R” which identifies an INSURV inspection as being the originator of the job. A list of all MMBU code can be found in the NAVSEALOGCEN website https://oars.nslc.navy.mil/oars/docs/mmbureferencelisting.html. b. Type Availability Code (TA Code). (1) TA Code 1. Depot level work candidate. When a unit receives or initiates a TA 1 job, the ship is accountable for ensuring the job is screened and brokered. The Port Engineer is responsible for the action of screening and brokering but the ship will track all TA 1 jobs to ensure they are scheduled for the next convenient availability. The status of all TA 1 jobs for the ship are identified in the Virtual Snap-Shot Report for commands visibility. (2) TA Code 2. IMA level work. When a unit receives or initiates a TA 2 job, the ship is accountable for ensuring the job is screened and brokered. The Port Engineer is responsible for the action of screening and brokering but the ship will track all TA 2 jobs to ensure they are scheduled for the next convenient availability. The status of all TA 2 jobs for the ship are identified in the Virtual Snap-Shot Report for commands visibility. (3) TA Code 3. Technical Assistance jobs. When a unit receives or initiates a TA 3 job, the ship is accountable for ensuring the job is screened and referred. The Port Engineer is responsible for the action of screening and referred but the ship will track all TA 3 jobs to ensure the jobs are brokered to a maintenance activity so the requested technical assistance can be provided. The status of all TA 3 jobs for the ship are identified in the Virtual Snap-Shot Report for commands visibility. (4) TA Code 4. CSMP work notifications that are within ship’s force capability to complete. A TA 4 job can originate from on the ship or an outside inspection team such as an INSURV or Total Ship’s Readiness Assessment.

TA 4 jobs will be sent to VSB via CSMP upline but the Port Engineer may not have visibility of the jobs. Additionally, a job may have been written by the ship as a TA 1 - 3 and the Port Engineer may screen the job as a TA 4. This will be reflected by the SPEAR Report or during the monthly CSMP Reconciliation Process. If a job is screened as a TA 4 the ship will change the TA Code of the job to 4. If the ship still desires an outside activity to perform the work, the Port Engineer should be notified. c. Equipment Status Code (ESC) and Equipment Operational Code (EOC). The ESC and EOC will reflect the actual condition of the equipment at the time the Work Candidate is created. The ESC from OMMS-NG units is used to compute the EOC which is a major factor in determining the mission operational capabilities of the ship. d. Safety Code. A safety Code will be added to all CSMP work candidates. If the job has no effect on the safety to personnel and/or equipment, a Safety Code of “0” will be utilized. The following safety codes are authorized for use: (1) “X”. Enter an "X" or applicable safety code if the maintenance action describes a problem or condition which has caused, or has the potential to cause serious injury to personnel or material. A brief explanation must be included in the Remarks/Description field (Block 35). For example: "RE-INSPECTION OF SEPARATOR FOR PRESENCE OF OIL AFTER RINSE. MRC A-27 EVIDENTLY NOT DONE. PRESENCE OF OIL RESULTED IN FIRE IN HP AIR SYSTEM WHEN COMPRESSOR OPERATED UNDER LOAD. FIRE BADLY BURNED VALVE AHP-287, REQUIRING REPLACEMENT." (2) “1”. Critical safety or health deficiency. Correct Immediately. (3) “2”. Serious Safety or Health deficiency. Suspension of Equipment, System or Space use is required. (4) “3”. Moderate Safety or health deficiency.

Waiver of Equipment, System or Space use is granted pending correction of the item. (5) “4”. Minor safety or health deficiency. (6) “5”. Negligible safety or health deficiency. (7) “0”. Maintenance action is not safety related. e. Block 10. TYCOM directs units to utilize block 10 as an attribute for jobs that have one or more of the characteristics below. If a corrosion or environmental job is found during a zone inspection, the corrosion or environmental status takes precedence. (1) “C”. All Corrosion jobs will be annotated with a “C” in Block 10. (2) “E”. All jobs having an environmental impact will have a “E” in block 10. (3) “Z”. All jobs discovered during Zone Inspection will annotated with a “Z” in block 10. f. Availability ID Code. A four-digit Alpha numeric code used to identify the availability a particular job has been assigned to. If the Availability ID Code is blank, it means the job has not yet been screened to an availability. NTCSS Failure And Recovery. a. NTCSS Failure. Report failure to Surface Force 3-M Representative and TYCOM 3MC. b. NTCSS Recovery. Conduct recovery process per NIWC directive and guidance. c. All ASIs and TYCOM bulkloads received during the outage will be installed per emailed files from TYCOM 3-M. If bulkloads cover a Total Ship’s Readiness Assessment event, those must be loaded by daily sequence files. Equipment Validations. The correct equipment configuration is the basis for all maintenance and supply support programs. Ship’s Force is in the best position to identify and make corrections to inaccuracies in equipment records when compared to the actual installed equipment. a. Each WC will perform equipment validations per the following priority and guidance. Corrective Maintenance. Prior to writing a work candidate, WCS will verify when the equipment was last validated. If not validated in the past 36 months, MP will validate the equipment record using validation aid provided by WCS.

Ships that are Pre-commission or in Service Life Extension Program will validate all equipment onboard to establish correct configuration until sail away for new construction or upon completion of Service Life Extension Program. b. Shipboard personnel will conduct validations by printing a hard copy validation aid from the installed MDS system unless full electronic devices are available. Validation aids contain information about the equipment including the WC owning the equipment for maintenance purposes, location, serial number, or Positional Reference Identification number. In addition, APL header data is included. These copies, if required, will be kept for 13 weeks or until electronic MDS system is verified correct. c. Paperless Equipment Validation process. (1) WCSs will print Equipment Validation Aid from OMMS-NG. (If command has portable laptops or hand-held computers then this can be disregarded.) (2) The MP will utilize the Equipment Validation Aid (if applicable) and conduct sight validation. (a) MP will locate equipment and verify APL Header data and Component Characteristics information (RIC information located on the left-hand side of validation aid). Any disparity will require a change in configuration request or Wrong in Model-Not in Model request to add the correct APL for equipment. If unable to verify due to missing label plate information, inaccessible, lagged over etc. equipment validation code will be sight validated without RIC and select correct reason why. If APL or characteristic data is correct, the equipment record will be sight validated with RIC. (b) MP will verify serial number is correct or annotate discrepancies. If serial number is not available, then utilize Positional Reference Identification. (c) MP will verify that the correct WC is listed, annotate discrepancies. (d) MP will verify the equipment is correctly associated to the correct PMS and the MIP and all associated MRCs will be annotated. (e) MP will sign and date validation aid. (If using portable laptop or hand-held computer, disregard.) (f) MP will return Equipment Validation Aid to WCS (if applicable).

MP or WCS (if using portable laptop or hand-held computer MP will update the record) can update configuration record notes section to ensure all annotations on the validation aid are transcribed over to the MDS record, along with MP name who conducted sight verification and the date in which the sight validation was conducted. PMS MIP and all associated MRCs will be annotated in the notes section of record as well. If PMS is required but not assigned to unit, then submit an FBR requesting additional coverage and document the FBR number in the notes section of the record. If no PMS is required, annotate No Maintenance Required in the notes section of the record. (3) The WCS will take the validation aid (if applicable) and ensure all information on validation aid is entered correctly in the notes section of the configuration record. (If portable laptop or hand-held computers utilized, the WCS will verify record). (4) CoC will review and approve all equipment configuration record changes. (5) The 3MC will be able to view all completed validations from the MDS via reports or list function in the applicable MDS. Figure 19-6-1 PLANNING BOARD FOR MAINTENANCE PB4M Meeting. Each unit will have a formally structured PB4M which should meet twice per month at a minimum. This forum provides a review of open Casualty Reports, current planned off-ship and organizational maintenance, CSMP quality and accuracy, future maintenance and modernization planning, and fiscal concerns. The objective of PB4M is to ensure clarity of intent for both the ship’s efforts and the shore infrastructure with respect to total ship maintenance, operational schedules, and other concerns affecting ship material readiness. The PB4M must include the CO (who will chair the meeting), XO, 3MC, all DH, SMMO, Port Engineer (PE), and additional personnel as desired (e.g., TYCOM Rep). PE Responsibilities. Quarterly the PE will assist the ship’s CO in conducting the PB4M meetings, including agenda development.

The SMMO will prepare the ship input to the PB4M agenda in support of the PE to include COMNAVSURFOR reconciliation tool and self-Sufficiency report results. PB4M Timing, Periodicity, And Agenda. Flexible to support the priorities of the individual ship and meet the unique maintenance requirements of each phase of the TYCOM Operational Fleet Response Plan. However, the Maintenance Team will have reviewed the CSMP in detail prior to PB4M, then discuss the CSMP during routine PB4Ms and prior to every maintenance availability. 19-6.6 3M 365 CONTINUOUS MONITORING Pillars Of Performance. There are four Pillars of Performance within the 3-M program. While the pillars may affect one another, each pillar must be evaluated independently. For units with multiple crews, all 3-M 365 Pillars of Performance will be measured by hull. a. Maintenance Accomplishment Rate (MAR). The Maintenance Accomplishment Rate is the amount of the scheduled or unscheduled maintenance that was accomplished. Scheduled maintenance is performed on a periodic basis while situational maintenance is performed based upon an event such as those identified in the Major Events Listing or when required while conducting a periodic check. b. Spot Check Program. The Spot Check Program is the Quality Assurance program for the maintenance conducted at subordinate commands. The purpose is to ensure the right maintenance is conducted on the right equipment safely and effectively. c. Consolidated Ship’s Maintenance Program. The CSMP program is the Navy’s process of documenting discrepancies to spaces and equipment. The program entails Equipment configuration, discrepancy identification, screening or brokering work, and recording when deficiencies have been corrected. d. Knowledge, Skills, and Experience. The KSE model is a way to gauge the knowledge, skills, and experience of the crew members that make up a work center, department, or command. This model creates a unit of measurement to ensure personnel have both the training and qualifications to execute the assigned duties. Additionally, the performance portion of the model identifies the “end result” of the KSE model.

Although a Sailor may be trained and qualified, an evaluation of 3-M programs and activities will measure how well the responsibilities are executed. For units with multiple crews, a specific Multi-Crew KSE will be utilized. The multi-Crew KSE form will be identical to the single crew KSE except each 3-M position will have two names. Periodic Reports. a. Virtual Snap-Shot Report (1) Overview. The Virtual Snap-Shot Report is a CNSF produced excel workbook that creates a 20-page graphical representation for the health of the MAR and Spot Check program pillars of performance. The report uses a drill down method to identify strengths and weaknesses with the two pillars. (2) Periodicity. This report is to be conducted weekly by all commands. (3) Required Documents. (a) PMS Analysis Spreadsheet. The PMS Analysis Spreadsheet is an excel workbook that contains a list of all periodic checks, situational checks, and alerts the command has recorded in SKED for the past quarter. The report is generated from the SKED Admin tab. The period of report will be period of 13 weeks, beginning on a Monday and ending on a Sunday. (b) Spot Check - All Report. The Spot Check - All Report from sked contains a list of all spot checks conducted during the last quarter with the associated grades for each of the spot checks. The report is generated from the Reports tab. The period of report will be period of 13 weeks, beginning on a Monday and ending on a Sunday. (4) Virtual Snap-Shot Report Breakdown (a) Cover Sheet. The cover sheet automatically fills in the ship’s name and date. The user will enter the following information for the command’s 3-M Program: 1 FR#. Enter the current Force Revision the SKED implemented at the commands. (Ex. 4-21, 1-22, 2-22) 2 3-M Cert Date. Enter the date for the last 3-M certification event. If the certification date is not known, contact your Fleet’s Afloat Training Group unit to provide. 3 CSMP Reconciliation Date. Enter the date of your last CSMP Reconciliation Report.

4 Number of Reconciliation Discrepancies. The total number of discrepancies identified during the last CSMP Reconciliation. 5 MAR Pillar. An automatically populated block that records the Maintenance Accomplishment Rate for the command. 6 Spot Check Pillar. An automatically populated block that records the Spot Check Accomplishment Rate for the command. 7 CSMP Pillar. A manually populated block to record the CSMP Management Score for the command. The CSMP Management Score can be found on the cover page of the CSMP Self-Sufficiency Report. 8 KSE. A Manually populated block to record the Knowledge, Skills, and Experience Score located on the Dashboard of the KSE Tool. This block is only applicable for commands that have transitioned from legacy 3-M Certification criteria to the 3-M 365 Continuously Monitored and Continuously Certified program. 9 Attachments. There are two mandatory attachments that must be submitted with the Virtual Snap-Shot Report: a IEM Details Report b Additional Attachments. Contains three empty spaces for voluntary attachments. 10 Acknowledgment blocks. Contains a place for the CO and XO to initial stating they have received the document and provides an area for comments if desired. b. PMS Performance Rate (PPR). The PPR page provides an overview of both the command’s MAR and Spot Check Average to create a PPR for the command and each of the departments within. c. Maintenance Accomplishment Summary. The Maintenance Accomplishment Summary provides a three-page executive level evaluation of the MAR for the command. The major sections of the report as follows: (1) Maintenance Accomplishment by Week Graph. A graphical representation of the MAR for the last 13 weeks. The graph provides a trend analysis for the command’s maintenance accomplishment. The Fleet requirement of 80% is identified by a red dotted line on the graph. (2) Departments for the Last Quarter. Each department at the command has the maintenance accomplishment number identified. The following metrics are used for evaluation: (a) # COMPL. The number of checks the Department has completed within the last 13 weeks. (b) # ALERTS.

The number of alerts represents the number of checks that were rescheduled due to non-accomplishment. Each alert signifies one check that was not accomplished. (c) # LOST. Checks that were scheduled and lost due to the inability to reschedule. Daily checks, or situationally required checks are unable to be rescheduled. (d) # NA. The number of checks that were scheduled and marked as Not Applicable. While NA checks do not affect the commands 3-M score, caution should be taken to ensure there actually were not applicable and not maintenance that should have been accomplished. (e) TOTAL # CHKS. This number is the sum of all checks completed, lost, and alerted during the 13-week period. (f) PAR%. The PAR Score is the Periodic Accomplishment Rate. The PAR Score represents the amount of periodically scheduled maintenance that was accomplished. (g) SAR%. The SAR Score is the Situational Accomplishment Rate. The PAR Score represents the amount of situationally scheduled maintenance that was accomplished. (h) WEIGHT%. The portion of overall command maintenance accomplished within a given Department. This weight is also used to determine the effect on the command MAR. (i) MAR%. The departments Maintenance Accomplishment Rate for the last 13 weeks. (3) Work Centers for the Last Quarter. This section is identical to the department section except data is for a specific Work Center over the last 13 weeks. (4) Alerts Report. A two-page section that graphically displays the command’s alerts over the last 13 weeks. It is important to understand that a check will not start alerting until the check is beyond its maximum scheduling range. For example, an A-1 check will not alert as soon as the check is due. The check can still be moved out 6 months. After 18 months the check will start alerting. The following sections are used to evaluate the command’s alerts: (a) Alerts by Week. A graphical representation for the number of alerts within the command over the last 13 weeks. This graph is used for trend analysis. (b) Number of alerts per Work Center. This is the number of alerts by work center for the previous week only.

If the cell next to the work center is blank, it means that work center had no alerts for the previous week. If the cell next to the work center has a number and another number in parenthesis, than the first number is the number of alerts for the previous week and the number in parenthesis represents the number of alerts that have been out of periodicity for 13 weeks in a row. Adding up the number of alerts for each of the work centers will equal the number of alerts for the last week as identified in the alerts by week graph. (c) Top 50 longest running alerts. This a list of alerts at the command that have been out of periodicity the longest. This may not be all of the alerts. Each alert has the following information: 1 # weeks alerted. This is the number of weeks in a row that the check has been out of periodicity. A 13 in the cell does not mean that the check has only been alerting for 13 weeks. Because the report only utilizes 13 weeks of data this is the maximum number that can be displayed. 2 WC. The Work Center that has responsibility for the maintenance check. 3 MIP. The Maintenance Index Page of the Check that is out of periodicity. 4 Periodicity. The periodicity of the check as identified by the maintenance card. 5 Equipment name. The equipment name as listed in the SKED equipment file. If equipment in SKED is properly associated to the CDMD-OA file, the equipment name will match between the two. d. Lost Checks Report. A two-page section that graphically displays the command’s lost checks over the last 13 weeks. The following sections are used to evaluate the command’s lost checks: (1) Lost Checks by Week. A graph displaying the number of lost checks per week for the last 13 weeks. This graph is utilized for trend analysis purposes. (2) Lost Checks by Work Center. The number of lost checks by work center for the last 13 weeks. This data enables commands to identify which work centers are not able to complete daily and situational maintenance checks. (3) Top 50 Equipment items with the most lost checks.

This is a list of the top 50 lost checks based upon the equipment and work center. Some equipment has more than one daily check or situational check associated to it. Below is a description of what the list provides: (a) WC. The work center that owns the piece of equipment that has lost checks associated to it. (b) # times lost. The number of daily or situational checks that have been lost for the piece of equipment. (c) Equipment. This is the equipment name as identified by the SKED equipment file. If the equipment is properly associated, the equipment name will be the same as the CDMD-OA database. (4) NA Checks Report. A two-page section that graphically displays the command’s Not Applicable checks over the last 13 weeks. Although NA checks are not counted against the command’s Maintenance Accomplishment Rate, the command should be aware of the checks marked NA as it could indicate maintenance that should have been accomplished and was not. The following sections are used to evaluate the command’s Not Applicable checks: (a) NA Checks by Week. A graph displaying the number of checks marked as not applicable over the last 13 weeks. This graph is used to show trend analysis for the command. (b) NA Checks by Work Center. The number of checks marked NA by work center over the last 13 weeks. (5) Top 50 Equipment items with the most NA checks. This is a list of the top 50 NA checks based upon the equipment and work center. Below is a description of what the list provides: (a) WC. The work center that owns the piece of equipment that has NA checks associated to it. (b) # times NA. The number of checks that have been marked as Not Applicable for the piece of equipment. (c) Equipment. This is the equipment name as identified by the SKED equipment file. If the equipment is properly associated, the equipment name will be the same as the CDMD-OA database. e. Spot Check Analysis Report. A summary of the Spot Check Program health via actionable metrics. Below is a description for each section of the report. (1) Number of Spot Checks per Week.

A graph that displays the number of Spot Checks conducted at the command over the last 13 weeks. The number includes both historical Spot Checks and Monitored Maintenance Spot Checks. (2) Department Spot Check Program Health. A list of each department and their respective Spot Check metrics. The fields are listed below: (a) Department. The Department Name. (b) # Spot Checks. The number of Spot Checks conducted within a given department for the last 13 weeks. This is a rollup metric for each of the work centers within a department. (c) # Fail. The number of spot checks that were marked as failures in SKED in the last 13 weeks. (d) Pass %. The percentage of Spot Checks that passed within a department. While commands may naturally desire a high pass percentage, a very high score may indicate Spot Checkers are not utilizing a critical eye. (e) Weight %. Weighting is used to calculate the weight of a given department score on the commands overall Spot Check Average. Weighting is based upon the amount of spot checks conducted in that department. (f) AVG Score %. The average spot check score achieved during the last 13 weeks. (3) Work Center Spot Check Program Health. A list of each Work Center and their respective Spot Check metrics. The fields are listed below: (a) Work Center. The Work Canter name. (b) # Spot Checks. The number of Spot Checks conducted within a given Work Center for the last 13 weeks. (c) # Fail. The number of spot checks that were marked as failures in SKED in the last 13 weeks. (d) Pass %. The percentage of Spot Checks that passed within a Work Center. (e) Weight %. Weighting is used to calculate the weight of a given Work Center score on the commands overall Spot Check Average. Weighting is based upon the amount of spot checks conducted in that Work Center. (f) AVG Score %. The average spot check score achieved during the last 13 weeks. (4) Top 10 Spot Checks Conducted. A list of the maintenance checks that were spot checked the most in the last 13 weeks. The “# of SCs” block indicates the number of times a spot check was completed.

Line items highlighted in green indicate a troubled system check as specified by TYCOM. These are checks mostly identified as leading to INSURV inspection discrepancies. (5) Toughest Spot Checkers. This list contains the names of the 10 personnel that have failed the most spot checks. The list will only contain the names of Spot Checkers that have conducted more than the average number of spot checks for the command and have failed at least one spot check. (6) The 100% Club. A list of Spot Checkers that have conducted the over the average number of spot checks and have found zero discrepancies. While grading one or more spot checks at 100% may be legitimate, this list may indicate personnel that need to have a more critical eye during spot checks. (7) Partial Spot Checkers. A list of personnel that have conducted one or more spot checks with a partial grade. CNSF does not authorize partial grading during spot checks. Each attribute on the Spot Check form is an all or nothing score. For Example, an attribute worth 10 points will either be 10, 0, or NA as applicable. A grade of 1 through 9 will not be used for any reason for this attribute. f. List of Failed Spot Checks. This is a list of spot checks that failed during the last week and the reason the check failed. Reason may be blank if the spot checker did not provide a comment. Because of the hard kill attributes on the spot check form, a person that partially grades a spot check may show up on this list even though they were unaware the spot check failed. g. Spot Check Completion Report. A list of the command spot checkers and the number of spot checks the personnel conducted for each week for the last 13 weeks. Because this list is derived directly from SKED data, the personnel paygrade is unavailable. Due to this limitation, the list is sorted based upon the number of historical checks conducted in the last 13 weeks. h. Spot Check Randomizer. A list of randomly selected checks to be spot checked for each work center that has conducted maintenance in the last 13 weeks.

Checks are randomly selected based upon periodicity, troubled system status, when the check was accomplished, and how many times the spot check was previously conducted. All units are directed to utilize the Spot Check Randomizer to the maximum extent possible. If a maintenance person or equipment is unavailable and the randomly selected check cannot be performed, the spot checker will select another check within that work center with a moderate level of difficulty. CSMP Reconciliation Report (OMMS). a. Overview. This report is used to identify discrepancies between the alignment of the OMMS and VSB databases. Alignment of the databases is critical to CSMP management to ensure the command and Port Engineer have the same situational awareness for the status of on-ship and off-ship work candidates. The results of the CSMP Reconciliation will be forwarded to the Surface Force 3-M Representative upon completion. b. Periodicity. The CSMP Reconciliation will be completed by all commands monthly by the fifth day of each month. c. Required Documents: (1) OMMS CSMP Export. A copy of active JSN residing on ship. (2) VSB Export. An export of the global report in VSB named “CNSF CSMP Reconciliation Report”. d. CSMP Reconciliation Report Breakdown: (1) Cover Sheet. The cover sheet of the report provides an executive level overview for alignment between the units OMMS database and the VSB database utilized by the Port Engineer to screen and broker work. Below are the sections of the report: (a) Total Number of Jobs in the Ship’s CSMP. The total number of active jobs in the ship’s CSMP. (b) Total Number of Jobs in VSB. The total number of active jobs in VSB. (c) CSMP Reconciliation Score. A calculation that represents how closely aligned the OMMS and VSB database are aligned. (2) CSMP Reconciliation Summary. A summary of discrepancies identified during the reconciliation process. Each discrepancy type has a independent list of jobs by JSN and Work Center that fall into the category. Below is a list of the discrepancies effect, the cause, and the corrective action needed: (a) Closed in VSB.

The number of jobs separated by those generated on-ship and off-ship that are closed in VSB but active on the ship’s CSMP. Jobs that show closed in VSB are no longer being updated by the Port Engineer. 1 Possible Cause. Jobs may have been reported to the Port Engineer and closed to reflect that status. 2 Corrective action. Ship’s force should review the job validity. If the job has been completed, the job should be marked as complete in OMMS. If the job is still active and needs to be complete, the Port Engineer will need to resurrect the job so it can be screened and brokered as needed. (b) Not in VSB. The number of jobs separated by those generated on-ship and off-ship that reside in the ship’s CSMP but are not in VSB. If a job is not in VSB than the Port Engineer does not see the job and it will not be screened or brokered. 1 Possible Cause. The unit may have inactivated and archived prior to performing an upline via RADWEB to VSB. If this happens, jobs will be archived and any updates will not be reflected in VSB. Jobs may be awaiting approval and have not made it to the 3MC. 2 Corrective Action. Ship’s Force should review the job for validity. If the job is still valid, the job will need to be “tickled” so the job will be sent to VSB during the next upline. “Tickling” the job means to make an update to the job. (c) Mismatch. The number of jobs separated by those generated on-ship and off-ship that are listed as TA 1-3 on the ship but are listed as TA 4 in VSB. This type of error leads the unit to believe that an outside activity will complete the work but the Port Engineer has stated that ship’s force will complete the work. 1 Possible Cause. Ship’s force wrote the job as a TA 1-3 and the Port Engineer screened the job back to ship’s force. 2 Corrective Action.

Ship’s force will need to change the TA code in OMMS to a TA 4 or communicate why the job is not within ship’s force capability and have the Port Engineer rescreen the job back to a TA 1-3. (d) TA 4 Not in OMMS. The number of TA 4 jobs separated by those generated on-ship and off-ship that reside in VSB but are not listed on the ship’s CSMP. 1 Possible Cause. The unit may have inactivated and archived prior to performing an upline via RADWEB to VSB. If this happens, jobs will be archived and any updates will not be reflected in VSB. Another possible cause is that a bulkload was sent to the ship from CNSF and was not loaded into OMMS. 2 Corrective Action. The job will need to be reviewed for validity. If the job is still valid, the job will need to be rewritten. Additionally, the Port Engineer will need to close the job in VSB. (e) TA 1-3 Not in OMMS. The number of TA 1-3 jobs separated by those generated on-ship and off-ship that reside in VSB but are not listed on the ship’s CSMP. 1 Possible Cause. The unit may have inactivated and archived prior to performing an upline via RADWEB to VSB. If this happens, jobs will be archived and any updates will not be reflected in VSB. Another possible cause is that a bulkload was sent to the ship from CNSF and was not loaded into OMMS. 2 Corrective Action. The job will need to be reviewed for validity. If the job is still valid, a list of the job/jobs missing will need to be sent to TYCOM 3-M team to generate a bulkload containing the missing jobs. (f) P.E. Action Needed. The number of jobs separated by those generated on-ship and off-ship that were reported to VSB as being customer completed and awaiting closure in VSB. TA 1-3 jobs are dual close jobs and require both the ship and the outside activity to report completion prior to the job closing in VSB. 1 Possible Cause.

The ship has marked the job as complete and reported that status to VSB via an upline. The outside activity has not yet reported the job as complete. 2 Corrective Action. Notify the Port Engineer that the jobs have been closed by ship’s force so they can get an updated status from the activity that completed the work. Port Engineer will need to close the job in VSB once activity reports status. (g) P.E. No Screening Required. The number of jobs separated by those generated on-ship and off-ship that are listed as TA 1-3 but have a WN status of “No Screening Required”. This means the job will not be screened or brokered by the Port Engineer. 1 Possible Cause. The job status was changed from “Screening Required” to “No Screening Required” in VSB. 2 Corrective Action. Notify the Port Engineer so they can change the job WN status back to “Screening Required” and screen/broker as needed. CSMP Reconciliation Report. a. Overview. This report is used to identify discrepancies between the alignment of the AWN, ATM and VSB databases. Alignment of the databases is critical to CSMP management to ensure the command and Port Engineer have the same situational awareness for the status of on-ship and off-ship work candidates. The results of the CSMP Reconciliation will be forwarded to the Surface Force 3-M Representative upon completion. b. Periodicity. The CSMP Reconciliation will be completed by all commands monthly by the fifth day of each month. c. Required Documents: (1) AWN CSMP Export. A copy of all JSNs residing on ship. (2) ATM CSMP Export. A copy of all JSNs residing on ship. (3) VSB Export. An export of the global report in VSB named “CNSF CSMP Reconciliation Report”. d. CSMP Reconciliation Report Breakdown. (1) Cover Sheet. The cover sheet of the report provides an executive level overview for alignment between the units AWN database, the shore ATM database, and the VSB database utilized by the Port Engineer to screen and broker work. Below are the sections of the report:

(a) Total Number of Jobs in the AWN. The total number of active jobs in the ship’s CSMP. (b) Total Number of Jobs in the ATM. The total number of active jobs in the AWN ashore CSMP. (c) Total Number of Jobs in VSB. The total number of active jobs in VSB. (d) Number of CSMP Discrepancies. A summation of the total number of discrepancies between all three CSMP databases. (2) CSMP Reconciliation Summary. A summary of discrepancies identified during the reconciliation process. Each discrepancy type has an independent list of jobs by JSN and Work Center that fall into the category. Below is a list of the discrepancies effect, cause, and corrective action needed: (a) Duplicate Jobs Same Problem. This is a list of jobs that are duplicated in the ATM database and have the same job description. Only one of these jobs’ statuses are being reflected in VSB. 1 Possible Cause. The most common cause is the Maintenance Figure of Merit system created a new job after ship’s force updates the status of a job. For example, a job gets closed by ship’s force but ATN creates a new duplicate job with the status of closed versus changing the status of an existing job. 2 Corrective action. Ship’s force should review the job validity. If the job has been completed, the job should be marked as complete in ATM. (b) Duplicate Jobs Different Description. A list of JSNs in ATM that have been duplicated by represent different corrective actions. Because there is a delay in transferring data between AWN and ATM, if jobs are being written directly to ATM there is a chance that ship’s force is writing a job in AWN at approximately the same time. This will create two jobs with the same JSN that have different corrective actions. (c) In AWN Missing from VSB and ATM. A job that resides on the ship in the AWN database but has not replicated in ATM. 1 Possible Cause. AWN Health was not monitored and connectivity loss led to data not being replicated off ship. 2 Corrective Action. Updating the job in AWN will allow the job to attempt replication off-ship.

(d) In ATM missing from VSB and AWN. These are typically bulkloaded (Off-Ship) jobs that did not replicate from the ATM database. 1 Possible Cause. Not maintaining AWN health and connectivity will prevent ATM from replicating to AWN. 2 Corrective Action. The job will need to be updated in ATM to force replication to AWN and VSB. (e) In ATM and AWN missing from VSB. Jobs from ATM did not replicate to VSB 1 Possible Cause. ATM may have loss connectivity or servers were down when upload was attempted. 2 Corrective Action. The job will need to be updated in either AWN or ATM to force replication to VSB. (f) In VSB missing from ATM and AWN. Jobs that reside in VSB but are not contained in either the AWN or ATM databases. 1 Possible Cause. Jobs may have been closed in AWN or ATM but the information did not reflect in VSB. Jobs may show as “Customer Completed” in VSB. TA 1-3 jobs require dual closure from both the command and maintenance activity. 2 Corrective Action. Notify the Port Engineer that the jobs have been closed by ship’s force so they can get an updated status from the activity that completed the work. Port Engineer will need to close the job in VSB once activity reports status. (g) In VSB and AWN missing from ATM. A job that is still active in AWN and VSB but not in ATM. 1 Possible Cause. The job was somehow closed in ATM but did not replicate to AWN or VSB. 2 Corrective Action. Modify the job in AWN to force replication to ATM. If the job still does not replicate than the existing job will need to be closed and rewritten. If the job is TA 1-3 and brokered by the Port Engineer to an active availability, the job can be bulkloaded back from VSB by TYCOM. (h) In VSB and ATM missing from AWN. A job that is still active in both VSB and ATM that does not reside in the command’s CSMP. 1 Possible Cause. AWN health prevented the ship from receiving updates from ATM.

2 Corrective Action. Check AWN Health and modify the job in ATM. This will force the job to replicate back to AWN. (i) Active in AWN closed in ATM. A job that is still active in AWN but shows closed or canceled in ATM. 1 Possible Cause. The job was closed in ATM but the job status did not replicate to AWN. 2 Corrective Action. If the job is verified to be complete, close the job in AWN. If the job is verified to still be open, close the job in AWN and rewrite the job. (j) Active in ATM closed in AWN. A job that was closed in AWN but the information did not replicate to ATM. 1 Possible Cause. AWN health prevented ATM from receiving AWN updates. 2 Corrective Action. If the job is verified to be complete, close the job in ATM. (k) Active in AWN closed in VSB. A job that is still active in the command’s CSMP but has been closed or canceled in VSB. 1 Possible Cause. The job was closed in VSB. This job will no longer receive updates in VSB. 2 Corrective Action. If the job is still open and valid than a new work candidate will need to be rewritten for the job. (l) Active in VSB closed in AWN. A job that is still active in the Port Engineer’s CSMP but has been closed or canceled by the command. 1 Possible Cause. A command not verifying AWN health may have led to AWN not replicating off ship and VSB not receiving updates. 2 Corrective Action. The command will need to verify the work has been completed and work with the Port Engineer to close the job in VSB. (m) Active in ATM closed in VSB. A job that still shows open and active in the AWN Ashore CSMP but has been closed or canceled by the Port Engineer in VSB. 1 Possible Cause. The job was closed in VSB. This job will no longer receive updates in VSB. 2 Corrective Action. If the job is still open and valid, the job will need to be closed in ATM and rewritten in AWN.

(n) Active in VSB closed in ATM. A job that is still active in the Port Engineer’s CSMP but has been closed or canceled by the command. 1 Possible Cause. A command not verifying AWN health may have led to ATM not reporting to VSB that the job was complete. 2 Corrective Action. The command will need to verify the work has been completed and work with the Port Engineer to close the job in VSB. (o) TA 4 in VSB, TA1-3 in ATM and TA 4 in VSB, TA1-3 in AWN. A job that the command is expecting outside assistance with but the Port Engineer believes that the command will correct. 1 Possible Cause. Although the command requested outside assistance, the Port Engineer changed the job status to being within the command’s capability. 2 Corrective Action. The command will need to communicate with the Port Engineer to identify the reason the job was changed to a TA 4. If the job is determined to not be within the command’s capability the Port Engineer will need to change the WN Status Code to “Screening Required” and broker as needed. If determined that the command will correct the discrepancy, the command will need to update the TA Code to 4 in AWN and take corrective action as needed. (p) TA 1-3 with No Screening Required. A job that has a TA Code of 1-3 in VSB but displays “No Screening Required” as the WN Status. 1 Possible Cause. Multiple updates to a job led to a discrepancy between the TA Code and WN Status. The Port Engineer may not see this job and corrective action will not occur. 2 Corrective Action. The Port Engineer will need to update the WN Status to “Screening Required” and screen/broker as needed. CSMP Self-Sufficiency Report. a. Overview. This Report provides an executive level understanding of the unit’s CSMP management. This report evaluates the CSMP Management Team as whole, to include the Port Engineer. The report is separated into two sections off-ship and on-ship CSMP management. b. Periodicity. This report is required monthly for all units. c. VSB Export.

The VSB export for this report utilizes the same export as the CSMP Reconciliation tool. VSB is the only data used for this report making the reconciliation process critical for the accuracy of this report. d. CSMP Self-Sufficiency Report Breakdown. (1) Cover page. The top of the page is dedicated to providing overall assessment scores for CSMP Management. (a) CSMP Self-Sufficiency Score. A percentage that combines the off-ship self-sufficiency score and on-ship self-sufficiency score with a weight of 30% and 70% respectively. On-ship CSMP management is held with a higher weight due to ship’s force being solely responsible for the TA 4 jobs within the CSMP. (b) Off-Ship CSMP Score. This score represents the management of TA 1-3 work candidates. The ability for a unit to ensure off-ship work is screened by the Port Engineer and brokered or referred to an active availability. (c) On-Ship CSMP Score. This score represents a unit’s ability to efficiently manage TA 4 work candidates. A heavy focus is placed on the length of time between when a TA 4 job is written to when the job is accomplished. Additional weighting is placed on jobs identified as safety related. (d) Departments CSMP Scores. Each department is independently evaluated for their respective ability to manage off-ship and on-ship work candidates. (2) Off-ship CSMP Self-Sufficiency Scores. The first page of this section evaluates each of the department’s ability to manage off-ship CSMP work candidates. From left to right TA 1, 2, and 3 codes are separately analyzed. Each TA code has the same categories for evaluation: (a) Actively Screened. This is the number of active TA 1, 2, or 3 work candidates within a department. (b) Awaiting screening. This is the number of active TA 1, 2, or 3 work candidates within a department that are waiting for screening by the Port Engineer. Only jobs that have been waiting for screening over 30 days are counted.

Commands should use this to initiate discussion with the Port Engineer to find out why jobs in the CSMP are still needing to be screened. (c) Assigned to Past Avails. This is the number of active TA 1, 2, or 3 work candidates within a department that are assigned to availabilities that have ended over 90 days from when the report was generated. A 90-day buffer was added to provide time for the Port Engineer to collect financials and close out the avail. Before the 90-day mark, the Port Engineer should move the job to another availability so the work can be completed. (d) Unfunded avail. An unfunded availability is a temporary availability created in VSB to provide port engineers a place to store jobs until they can be assigned to an active availability. The Maintenance Data System (MDS), per the requirements of reference (a), provides maintenance and material managers throughout the Navy with the means to plan, acquire, organize, direct, control and evaluate man-power and material resources expended or planned for expenditure in support of maintenance. It allows for information collected by maintenance personnel to be recorded only once, and thereafter, the maintenance database will provide information to all who have a need for it.

Organizational (O-level) MDS requirements require the reporting of maintenance actions and configuration changes on all categories of equipment. Reference (b) provides specific guidelines for aircraft carriers. SPECIFIC REQUIREMENTS AND POLICY. a. Standard Force Work Center Numbering System. The production of automated products in support of the Ships’ Maintenance and Material Management (3-M) system, as well as the various automated maintenance information systems, dictate that a standard force work center (WC) organization be maintained. Commanding Officers (CO) will designate their command organization and applicable WC codes as reflected on the Joint Fleet Maintenance Manual (JFMM) website at https://www.navsea.navy.mil/Home/SUBMEPP/Products/JFMM/ under TYPE Commander (TYCOM) Documents and Forms. Additionally: (1) Commands must not allow the use of any WC codes not authorized by this manual. (2) Requests to change WC designation codes will not be approved unless they are applicable to all ships of a class and supported by detailed justification. WC change requests are routed to and approved by the U.S. Fleet Forces 3-M Requirements Management Board. This does not affect the re-assignment of a Maintenance Index Page (MIP) to another WC to effect shift of maintenance responsibility. Reference (a) and the feedback section of each TYCOM 3-M subchapter provide guidance for the shift of maintenance responsibility. (3) Small boat, tug, receiver, and service craft managers will use the specific WCs identified on the JFMM website at https://www.navsea.navy.mil/Home/SUBMEPP/Products/JFMM/ for MDS documentation. However, for Planned Maintenance System (PMS) management they may assign a “**00” WC to consolidate Periodic Force Revisions, MIPs, scheduling, etc., (e.g., PY30 through PY84 may consolidate PMS under WC PY00 or PY01-Mechanical, PY02-Electrical, etc.). The Unit Identification Code (UIC) will be that of the parent command.

(4) Standard Master Job Catalog (MJC) assigned WC codes (Surface Force ships and submarines only) are reflected in appendix A of this subchapter. b. Job Control Number. The Job Control Number (JCN) is the key identifier for maintenance actions and related supply documents. The JCN is used to identify a maintenance action and to relate all parts used when a ship reports a maintenance action complete. The JCN allows for consolidated reporting of all associated actions taken for the specific maintenance action. The JCN is comprised of three blocks as defined by the ship’s 3-M Manual. (1) Block 1 is the ship’s UIC (5 numeric characters). (2) Block 2 is the WC (4 alphanumeric characters, left justified). (3) Block 3 is the Job Sequence Number (JSN), usually 4 numeric characters. c. Job Sequence Number. The first position of the JSN is used to identify the tool or organization that created the “Preparation Instructions Maintenance Action Form (OPNAV 4790/2K)” (2-Kilo). If an outside activity creates a job for a ship, e.g., an Intermediate Maintenance Activity (IMA) creates an I-level repair action for a ship, the first character of the JSN will be an “Alpha” character. The control over which organizations or tools “OWN” which “ALPHA” character(s) is provided by the job originator values, appendix B of this subchapter, defined within the Maintenance and Modernization Business Unit and is available through the Naval Sea Logistics Center (NAVSEALOGCEN) web site under Maintenance and Modernization Business Unit look up tables. The specific value contained within the first position of the JSN provides enhanced data mining capabilities and facilitates data aggregation and analysis. CONFIGURATION DATA MANAGER. a. A Configuration Data Manager (CDM) for legacy UNNPI platforms, and Configuration Status Manager (CSM) for all platforms that have moved to Model Based Product Support (MBPS) is designated as the control authority for accuracy and completeness of the configuration information for each unit. A CDM may perform this function for multiple ships, submarines, and shore activities.

Prior to MDS delivery, the System Command (SYSCOM) and the delivering activity are responsible for reviewing and ensuring the initial accuracy and completeness of configuration data provided to the CDM. After delivery, which is the initial CDM validation, each CDM will maintain, update and modify its configuration data in MBPS. Navy Product Lifecycle Management (N-PLM) is the overarching Logistics Information Technology (LOG IT) solution replacing legacy applications including the Configuration Data Manager’s Database – Open Architecture and Revised Alternative Dataflow WEB (RADWEB) under digital transformation. MBPS is the maritime component of N-PLM and is comprised of three primary capabilities: (1) Navy Product Data Management (NPDM), (2) Navy Common Readiness Model (NCRM) (3) Navy Data Acquisition Requirements Tool (NDART) . b. NPDM’s role is to manage configuration, sustain and provide enterprise access to all components of legacy and future standards-based Navy Weapon System Technical Data Packages to include both weapon system configuration and technical data integrated and management within a singular N-PLM environment. Accordingly, NPDM supports the Ship Configuration and Logistic Support Information System (SCLSIS) process and data requirements in the same fashion as the legacy applications. However, it accomplishes this using an integrated data architecture with ties configuration and supporting technical data together holistically within a single NPLM solution. CONFIGURATION WORTHY ITEM. SCLSIS data requirements include documenting and maintaining all records associated with the design, supportability analysis, installation, test, certification, operation, assessment, inspection, maintenance, modernization and support of shipboard and shore-based equipment. Data requirements also include material, services and manpower associated with acquisition and sustainment. All identified Configuration Worthy Item (CWI) must be organized within the standard top-down breakdown hierarchically structured functional tiers approved for the ship or shore site in accordance with reference (f). An object is considered to be a CWI if it meets one or more of the following criteria: a. Any object that supports or requires any one of the following elements of logistics: (1) Supply support (APL or AEL worthy).

(2) Test and repair equipment, technical manuals and, or repair standards, Master Job Catalog (MJC) Routines, Periodic Maintenance Requirements (PMR), Software Programs (SWP), Software Control Manuals, Computer Program Packages, Maintenance Assistance Modules, Pack-up Kits, Deep Submergence System Hull Integrity Procedure Unrestricted Operations, intermediate or depot level maintenance plans, class maintenance plans or drawings (e.g., installation or configuration control drawings and ship selected records). (3) Objects associated with Training Requirements (shore test plants, ashore training units and ashore or afloat simulators). (4) Bill of Material on Ship Installation Drawings (SID), Weight and Moment Data, Ship Selected Record Data, Interface Control Data, Ship System Status Program (SSSP) Report Data and objects associated with Engineering Calculations, Logistics Supportability Analysis Record/Logistics Product Data. May also include Reliability Centered Maintenance (RCM), Failure Mode and Effects Analysis / Failure Mode, Effects and Criticality Analysis, Fault Tree Analysis. (5) PMS Maintenance Requirement Cards (MRC). Item’s that have an MRC but would not be considered configuration worthy for any other reason, may or may not be configuration worthy. Appendix J addresses the process for identifying maintenance and an item’s configuration worthiness. b. Any hardware, software or firmware item required to describe a ship’s or shore’s functional hierarchy. This results in a top-down breakdown hierarchical identification of all configuration items that are significant from a ship’s or shore maintenance and/or logistics perspective. Further guidance for software or firmware is included in Appendix H of reference (f). c. Any clearly identifiable functional assemblies such as pump/motor combinations (e.g., “Lube Oil Service Pump Assembly” composed of pump, coupling, motor, and controller), hydraulic manifolds, and air pressure reducing manifolds, etc. d. Any functional groups such as fitting groups, radio transmitter groups, network enclave etc. e. Any system or equipment that interfaces with an existing system or equipment already considered a CWI. f. Any system or equipment requiring “corrective” maintenance submitted via Maintenance Figure of Merit (MFOM) Automated Work Notification (AWN). g.

Any object (structure, system, equipment, component, sub-component, part, etc) requiring a Danger or Caution Tag Out or an object that supports a tag out (i.e., tag hung on it). h. Any device or object having maintenance information (e.g., material history, meter readings, parametric data taken in support of testing, operation and reporting material condition) recorded on it (e.g., Selected Equipment Records). Automated systems have been developed to reduce the administrative workload associated with shipboard reporting of maintenance. These databases provide users with responsive and flexible systems for on-line management of maintenance and to improve the accuracy and timeliness of existing up-line reporting. The following provides a high-level overview of the process. For a more detailed in-depth explanation, refer to reference (f), part A and Appendix A a. 3-M System Historical Database. The NSLC 3-M System Database is the focal point for receipt and distribution of unclassified maintenance and material data. Each reporting activity must ensure that narrative data sent up-line to this database does not contain any classified or Navy Nuclear Propulsion Information (NNPI). b. Model Based Product Support Navy Product Data Management (MBPS – NPDM). The MBPS-NPDM will ultimately replace the Legacy CDMD-OA, and non-authoritative configuration systems as the authoritative configuration status accounting system, to improve configuration and logistics management and control processes for Navy ships, submarines, and shore activities. Initially, MBPS-NPDM does not currently support those activities having U-NNPI data. Those activities will be maintained in CDMD-OA until such time NAVSEA 08 approves a MBPS U- NNPI solution. Through the implementation of Windchill, a Product Life Cycle Management application, NPDM integrates logistics data, processes, workflows, and people across the Navy enterprise and the Navy to support the management of information through the life cycle of systems and equipment in the fleet. This will provide enterprise access to all components of legacy with supported capabilities that include Configuration Management. c. The Process for an OMMS-NG or Non-Automated Work Notification afloat unit is initiated when the activity submits Current Ship’s Maintenance Plan (CSMP) up-line reports with equipment and configuration change transactions via JTDI in accordance with their TYCOM schedule.

The CSMP flows to the MFOM data center, where the configuration change data (OPNAV 4790/CK) is then forwarded to MBPS via the MBPS enhanced SDIF UI file import utility provided by ESB (Enterprise Service Bus). MBPS receives the data from ESB, reformats into a Standard Data Interface Format (SDIF-750) and then disseminates it to the appropriate CDM as a Work File Change Notice for review and processing in MBPS by the CDM. After the data has been reviewed and processed by the CDM, it then becomes available as an Automated Shore Interface (ASI) file made available to the unit via their JTDI mailbox. d. AWN activities do not generate CSMP files. Rather, they generate a “Not In Model (NIM)/Wrong In Model (WIM)” file and a separate file containing OPNAV 4790-2 Kilo data. The NIM/WIM data is replicated from the activity’s AWN database to the MFOM data center’s AWN database, reformatted, and passed to MBPS via the MBPS enhanced SDIF UI file import utility provided by ESB. MBPS receives the data from ESB, reformats it into a Standard Data Interface Format (SDIF-750) and then disseminates it to the appropriate CDM as a Work File Change Notice for review and processing in MBPS by the CDM. Once the NIM/WIM data is processed in MBPS, it then becomes available for MFOM (via the SDIF outbound process) to pull the data for the purposes of updating the MFOM model editor and AWN database at the MFOM data center and subsequent replication to the activity’s AWN database. Non-MFOM shore sites will use DPAS to track as until merged into MFOM and MBPS, all NAVIFOR sites will use MFOM/MBPS for tracking CWI equipment.
